content.intro: This lesson develops topic 155 of the supplied curriculum: **Masked Arrays**. The main starting point is **- The numpy.ma  module**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Specialized arrays represent data whose structure is not captured by a plain homogeneous numeric array. Choose the representation intentionally and document missing-value semantics.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Masked Arrays** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **- The numpy.ma  module** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.ma.array([10.0, 99.0, 20.0], mask=[False, True, False])
print(values.mean())

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: A masked array stores a data array and a mask describing invalid/hidden entries. Some consumers may drop the mask during conversion, so state the missing-data policy.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming object/string/date data behave like floats
common_mistakes.why: Different dtypes provide different operations and semantics.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect dtype and select matching routines.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating masked values as automatically removed everywhere
common_mistakes.why: Masked-array behavior depends on the operation and conversion boundary.
common_mistakes.fix: Check how downstream libraries treat masks and missing values.
